stages.script: Start with the anatomy, because the anatomy makes the emergency algorithm logical. A child with a tracheostomy may have two possible routes for air to reach the lungs. Route one is the normal upper airway, through the nose or mouth, larynx and trachea. Route two is directly through the stoma and tracheostomy tube. The crucial point is that the upper route may be completely usable, partly usable, or not usable at all. So before anything goes wrong, know whether this child has a patent upper airway. In an emergency, that one fact tells you whether face-mask ventilation or oral intubation could rescue oxygenation if the tracheostomy route fails.

Why are we more cautious with a fresh tracheostomy? Because in the first week, the stoma is not yet a mature tunnel. There is an opening through the skin and another opening into the trachea. If the tube comes out, those openings can become misaligned. A replacement tube may then pass into the soft tissues instead of the tracheal lumen. Maturation sutures help bring the trachea towards the skin and keep the openings aligned. Stay sutures are an additional rescue aid if an early tube change becomes necessary. But remember the important nuance. Avoiding an early change is a safety principle, not an absolute rule. If the tube is completely blocked and the child cannot breathe through it, leaving the blocked tube in place is also dangerous.

Most of the major problems with a new tracheostomy declare themselves early. You are looking for tube obstruction or displacement, pneumothorax, surgical emphysema and significant bleeding. Use the child, not just a monitor. Look at work of breathing and chest movement. Listen for airflow and breath sounds. Feel the chest and the neck. Surgical emphysema can produce swelling of the neck, face or upper chest, and a characteristic crackling sensation under the skin. Even a simple change in how tight the tracheostomy tapes feel can be an early clue that the neck is swelling. The saturation monitor matters, but supervision and direct observation may identify trouble earlier.

Prevention is part of emergency management. A tracheostomy bypasses the nose, so inspired gas loses normal warming and humidification. Paediatric tubes also have a very small internal diameter. Dry secretions therefore narrow the airway quickly. Good humidification, adequate hydration, appropriate nebulisation when prescribed and regular suction help keep the tube patent. Suction only to the prescribed tube length, because repeated trauma beyond the end of the tube can cause bleeding and granulation. Check the tapes because they are securing an airway, not simply holding a dressing. And keep the emergency equipment with the child. Knowledge is useless if the replacement tube is in another room.

When a child with a tracheostomy suddenly deteriorates, do not automatically attach a bag and start ventilating. First get help moving and give oxygen. Then answer two questions. Is the tube actually in the stoma and trachea? And is it patent? Look directly at the neck. Then pass the suction catheter to the expected distance. If the catheter passes and there is good airflow, move on through breathing and circulation. A tracheostomy is a common cause of acute deterioration, but it is not the cause of every deterioration. The danger is becoming so focused on the tube that you miss shock, bleeding or another respiratory problem.

If the suction catheter will not pass, decide whether this is partial or complete obstruction. If the child is still moving air and is relatively stable, especially with a fresh tracheostomy, try to clear the tube with suction, humidity and prescribed nebulisation rather than rushing into an unnecessary early tube change. But if the child is cyanosed, apnoeic or cannot ventilate, and the tube is completely blocked, the obstruction has to be relieved. Call for emergency and ENT help and prepare to change or remove the tube. Never assume that bagging through a blocked tube is ventilating the lungs.

If the tube is out and you cannot replace it, return to the original mental model. Does the child have a usable upper airway? If yes, you still have a route from the face to the lungs. Give oxygen there, and if bag-mask ventilation is needed, occluding the stoma can reduce gas escaping through the neck. If there is no usable upper airway, the stoma is the only route, so replacement and stoma ventilation become much more urgent. In a fresh tracheostomy, do not repeatedly force a tube through a tract that will not accept it. If you are successfully oxygenating by another route, keep oxygenating and let expert airway help solve the tract problem.

Surgical emphysema is simply air in the soft tissues where it should not be. The important mechanism is pressure. If there is a gap around a fresh stoma, or if a tracheostomy tube is displaced into a false passage, positive-pressure ventilation can drive air into the tissue planes of the neck and chest instead of into the lungs. The neck and face may swell and the skin can feel like bubble wrap. If surgical emphysema appears or rapidly worsens while you are bagging, question whether the tube is actually intratracheal. Continuing high-pressure ventilation through a false passage can make the problem dramatically worse.

Two further complications are easy to miss if all your attention stays on the tube. Pneumothorax may cause acute hypoxia, reduced or asymmetrical air entry and difficulty ventilating even though the tracheostomy itself is patent. Significant respiratory compromise is an emergency. Bleeding also needs context. A small amount of blood staining can occur after a new surgical airway, but ongoing or significant bleeding is different and needs urgent expert review. If there is an accessible external bleeding point, direct pressure may help while senior and surgical support is mobilised.

Before an emergency, know exactly what is in the child's neck. Know the size, length and type of tracheostomy, whether it is cuffed or uncuffed, the cuff system if present, the prescribed suction depth and what replacement tubes are in the emergency box. An inflated cuff usually has to be deflated before a cuffed tube can be removed, but different cuff systems behave differently, so tube-specific information matters. Also know whether a specialist tube has imaging restrictions. The bedside tube chart is not paperwork. It is emergency airway information.

Now put the reasoning together. It is day two after tracheostomy. The child becomes distressed, the saturation falls and the suction catheter stops halfway down the tube. Gentle suction does not clear it and the child becomes cyanosed. Treat this as critical obstruction while emergency help is coming. Because the tracheostomy is fresh, removal carries a risk of losing the immature tract or entering a false passage. But a completely obstructed tube is not ventilating the child. If the tube is removed and cannot be replaced, the fact that this child has a patent upper airway gives you a second rescue route. If neck swelling and crepitus then appear during an attempted reinsertion, think false passage and air tracking into soft tissues. Stop assuming that pressure delivered at the neck is reaching the lungs. Preserve oxygenation by the route that works.

Bring the whole session down to six questions. Why does this child have a tracheostomy, and do they have a usable upper airway? Is the tube actually in the trachea? Is it patent? Is the tract fresh or established? Which route can currently deliver oxygen to the lungs? And if the tracheostomy is in place and patent, what else is wrong? That is the MeducateMe version of the emergency algorithm. Do not memorise suction, change and bag as a ritual. Understand the anatomy, prove where the air is going, and preserve oxygenation while expert help is mobilised.
